final_candidates.decision_summary: Lysine 119 forms the internal aldimine (Schiff base) with the PLP cofactor; substituting arginine prevents covalent PLP attachment while preserving charge and overall fold. This is a direct, well-established catalytic ablation for CBS loss-of-function.

T257 is an active-site threonine and T257I is a known pathogenic missense mutation causing homocystinuria via severe CBS deficiency. Replacing the catalytic hydroxyl with isoleucine abolishes activity while the conservative hydrophobic change limits fold disruption.

C52 is a ligand of the N-terminal heme in human CBS; Cys-to-Ser removes the thiolate ligand, disrupting the heme environment required for catalysis. Loss of heme coordination strongly impairs activity with modest structural impact.

stop_reason.detail: Top-3 candidates are already the best-supported loss-of-function substitutions and no external evidence is available in this condition.

history.rationale: Cys52 is a key axial heme ligand in the N-terminal heme-binding region; replacing it with serine disrupts heme coordination and abolishes CBS activity while retaining the fold.

C52 is a documented active-site cysteine in CBS whose mutation (e.g., C52S) severely impairs PLP-dependent catalysis while retaining fold. Catalytic-site substitution directly serves loss-of-function objective.
Lys119 forms the internal aldimine with the PLP cofactor in the active site; mutation to arginine prevents PLP attachment, eliminating catalysis.

K119 forms the internal aldimine (Schiff base) with PLP; conservative K->R abolishes covalent cofactor attachment while preserving charge and fold. This is arguably the strongest single catalytic ablation.
His65 contributes to heme binding/active-site architecture; alanine substitution is expected to severely impair enzyme activity.
H65 participates in the catalytic machinery near the PLP site; alanine substitution disrupts catalysis without gross structural disruption.
Gly307 is a recurrent pathogenic missense hotspot in homocystinuria patients causing strong loss of CBS function, likely by disrupting the PLP-domain catalytic core.
G307 sits in the active-site region; Gly->Ser is a moderately disruptive substitution that could impair substrate channel but risk to fold is uncertain.
Ile278Thr is a classic patient-derived CBS mutation that markedly reduces activity (aggravated by B6), supporting a loss-of-function effect.
Retained as possible active-site-adjacent perturbation, but effect on catalysis is less direct than cofactor or catalytic residue mutations.
Thr257Ile is a known patient-associated B6-responsive variant with substantially reduced activity; conservative enough to keep protein viable.
T257 is part of the catalytic architecture (T257 is a known active-site threonine); Thr->Ile removes the catalytic hydroxyl. Confidence kept below top candidates due to fold risk.
Glu302Lys is a reported pathogenic CBS variant in the catalytic domain likely perturbing active-site electrostatics and lowering activity.
Charge reversal could destabilize local structure but catalytic linkage is indirect; downgraded mentally but retained for later comparison.
